title: Warm clothes: what works wet, and where nobody else looks
summary: Wool, fleece and other synthetics keep you warm when damp; cotton and down don't. Dress in layers, wear mitts rather than gloves in hard cold, keep a hat over the ears, and wear boots that aren't tight. Look for more in lost-and-found boxes, charity shops, linen rooms and back rooms, but never reach or climb into a clothing donation bin: people have died trapped in them.

steps.text: Put on what you have in layers: a base layer that insulates and pulls sweat off the skin (wool, polyester or polypropylene), loose warm middle layers that are easy to open or take off, and a windproof outer layer, waterproof if it's wet out. Each layer should be bigger than the one under it, so it doesn't squash it (CCOHS cold working).

Swap cotton next to the skin for wool or synthetics as soon as you can, and keep down dry: wet cotton and wet down stop insulating (CCOHS cold working, UA Sea Grant). Take a layer off before you sweat, and change out of anything wet straight away (Health Canada extreme cold).

Feet: dry boots that aren't tight, and either one thick pair of socks or a thin liner sock under a bigger thick one. Change out of wet socks as soon as you can (Health Canada extreme cold, Parachute winter).
steps.warn: Socks that are too thick make the boot tight and squeeze the foot, which slows the blood and makes cold injury more likely (CCOHS cold working, Parachute winter).

steps.text: Hands and head: mitts whenever you don't need your fingers, and always below about −17 °C (1 °F) (CCOHS cold working). A hat that keeps the ears warm (CCOHS cold working), and a scarf over the nose in wind (Health Canada extreme cold).
Then look for more where nobody else does: charity shops, lost-and-found boxes, dry cleaners, linen rooms, costume stores and the back rooms of clothing shops (table below).
Never reach into, look into or climb into a clothing donation bin, alone or not. Leave the bin alone and go to the charity's shop or warehouse instead.
steps.warn: At least eight people died in Canadian donation bins from 2015 to early 2019, trapped while climbing or reaching in (Global News bins, UBC Okanagan bins).

steps.text: Near a stove, candle or lamp, wear wool or cotton on the outside. Fleece and other synthetics can melt onto skin if worn too close to heat (UA Sea Grant, [Open flames](#browse/hazards/open_flame)).

notes:
## Which fabrics stay warm wet

Clothing keeps you warm by holding still air. Water fills those spaces and carries heat away, so what matters is how a fabric behaves when it gets damp from sweat, snow or rain (UA Sea Grant, CCOHS cold working).

| Fabric | Dry | Damp or wet | Near a flame |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wool | Good insulator | Loses some warmth, gets heavy, still keeps heat (UA Sea Grant, CCOHS cold working) | Not readily flammable (UA Sea Grant) |
| Fleece, pile, polyester, polypropylene | Good, light, dries fast | Keeps most of its warmth (UA Sea Grant) | Melts and burns holes; can stick to skin (UA Sea Grant) |
| Cotton: jeans, sweatshirts, flannel | Fine for a dry day | Soaks up water, no insulation, clammy (UA Sea Grant, CCOHS cold working) | Burns, but doesn't melt onto skin ([Open flames](#browse/hazards/open_flame)) |
| Down | One of the most efficient insulators for its weight (UA Sea Grant) | No insulation, and very hard to dry (UA Sea Grant) | Check the shell fabric |
| Silk | Thin | Loses its warmth (UA Sea Grant) | |
| Fur | Excellent; sheds frost and ice (UA Sea Grant) | Naturally water-resistant while its oils last (UA Sea Grant) | |

So the rule is wool or synthetics next to the skin and for anything you'll sweat in, a down jacket or sleeping bag only where it will stay dry, and cotton only as a dry, outer layer near a stove. Cotton isn't poison; wet cotton with nothing dry to change into is the problem.

## Layering

- Several layers hold more air than one thick garment, and you can add or shed them as you work and rest (UA Sea Grant, Parachute winter, CCOHS cold working).
- **Base:** insulates and wicks sweat off the skin: wool, polyester or polypropylene thermal underwear (CCOHS cold working).
- **Middle:** loose enough to hold warm air, easy to open or take off: sweaters, fleece, vests, a second wool shirt (UA Sea Grant, CCOHS cold working).
- **Outer:** stops wind; waterproof in wet snow and rain. Windproofing makes the layers under it work (UA Sea Grant, CCOHS cold working).
- Take a layer off before you sweat; add one when you stop (Health Canada extreme cold). Clothing next to the body gets wet from sweat and its insulation drops sharply (CCOHS cold working).
- For staying warm in the house and in bed, see [Staying warm](#guides/skill_staying_warm). For who gets cold fastest and how to tell, see [Cold indoors](#guides/reference_indoor_cold).

## Feet, hands and head

**Feet**
- For heavy work in cold, CCOHS suggests felt-lined boots with rubber bottoms, leather tops and removable felt insoles, and notes that leather lets sweat escape (CCOHS cold working). The removable liners and insoles can come out to dry overnight.
- Waterproof rubber boots are what you need in slush and water, but they hold sweat in (CCOHS cold working). Change socks more often in them.
- Socks: one thick pair, or a thin liner sock under a bigger thick one. Polypropylene liners pull sweat away from the skin (CCOHS cold working). Wool or wool-blend, not cotton (Parachute winter).
- Room to wiggle the toes. Boots or socks that squeeze the foot slow the blood and make cold injury more likely (CCOHS cold working, Parachute winter).

**Hands**
- CCOHS says gloves below 4 °C (39 °F) for light work and below −7 °C (19 °F) for moderate work, and mittens below −17 °C (1 °F) (CCOHS cold working). Mitts are what you wear in a real Canadian cold snap; gloves are for when you need your fingers.

**Head and face**
- A hat that keeps the ears warm (CCOHS cold working), and a scarf over the nose in wind (Health Canada extreme cold). For children at play, a tube neck warmer is safer than a scarf, which can strangle (Parachute winter).

## Where to look

Clothing shops are emptied early, but their fittings and back rooms often aren't (see [Small shops](#browse/buildings/shop_small), [Malls](#browse/buildings/mall)). The places below are where warm clothes sit that nobody thinks of. Check a building is safe before you go in: [Entering buildings](#guides/safety_entering_buildings).

| Place | What to look for |
|---|---|
| [Charity and second-hand shops](#browse/buildings/department) | Wool sweaters, coats, boots and blankets, often bagged and unsorted in the back |
| [Schools and colleges](#browse/buildings/school) | Lost-and-found bins near the office or gym: coats, hats, mitts, boots |
| [Arenas and rinks](#browse/buildings/stadium), [gyms](#browse/buildings/gym) | Lost and found, dressing rooms, pro shops: toques, gloves, hoodies, socks |
| [Train and transit stations](#browse/buildings/train_station), [bus depots](#browse/buildings/bus_depot) | Lost property offices. BC Transit keeps items up to 14 days, then gives them to charity (BC Transit lost and found), so expect recent things only |
| [Dry cleaners](#browse/buildings/laundromat) | Racks of finished, uncollected garments: wool coats, suits, parkas |
| [Hotels and motels](#browse/buildings/hotel) | Linen rooms: duvets, blankets, bathrobes; lost and found |
| [Hospitals](#browse/buildings/hospital), [nursing homes](#browse/buildings/nursing_home) | Linen rooms and blanket warmers: cotton blankets, flannel sheets, scrubs (fine as dry layers) |
| [Churches and community halls](#browse/buildings/church) | Clothing cupboards, rummage-sale stock, scout and guide halls |
| [Farm supply](#browse/buildings/farm_supply), [hardware](#browse/buildings/hardware) | Work gloves, insulated boots, coveralls, hand warmers |
| [Campgrounds](#browse/buildings/campground), [marinas](#browse/buildings/marina) | Camp stores, lost and found, rain gear |
| [Self storage](#browse/buildings/self_storage), [houses](#browse/buildings/house) | Winter clothes stored off-season in totes and closets |

And places with no card of their own:
- **Ski hills:** rental shops, lost and found, staff and patrol rooms.
- **Costume and theatre stores and wardrobes:** wool coats, cloaks, fur and felt.
- **Workwear and uniform stores:** insulated coveralls, parkas, lined work boots, mitts.
- **Hunting, fishing and outfitting stores:** wool, insulated boots and mitts, hand warmers.
- **Military surplus shops** are on the small-shops card: wool blankets and wool trousers.

Wash or air found clothes, and dry them in the warm room, never on the stove or heater (see [Safe indoor heating](#ref/reference_fire_heat/safe_indoor_heating)).

## Donation bins: don't reach in, don't climb in

The metal clothing bins in car parks are built like a mailbox, with a flap inside to stop arms reaching the clothes, and people who reach or look in can get trapped (Global News bins).
- At least eight people died after getting stuck in clothing donation bins in Canada from 2015 to January 2019, among them a man in Calgary (July 2017), a 32-year-old man in Cambridge, Ont. (November 2018), a woman in Vancouver (July 2018), a 34-year-old man in West Vancouver (late 2018, more than a week before the Toronto death) and a woman in Toronto (January 2019), which Global News counted as the eighth (Global News bins).
- People were climbing inside to collect clothes, and some got trapped and died for lack of air. The UBC Okanagan task-force lead says most incidents happen between 10 p.m. and 8 a.m., which he bases on anecdotal evidence (UBC Okanagan bins).
- In New Jersey in 2015, a 58-year-old man reaching into a bin for clothing lost his balance, got wedged in the opening and died of compression of the neck (NBC New York bin).
- After the deaths, the City of Vancouver said about 90% of its bins had been removed, and the maker of many Canadian bins stopped making the metal ones while it worked on safer designs (Global News bins).

So: don't reach, look or climb into a bin's chute at all. The clothes from these bins go to the charity's shops and sorting warehouses ([Warehouses](#browse/buildings/warehouse), [charity shops](#browse/buildings/department)), which are safer places to look.
